claim: The VPS13A gene is associated with the neurodegenerative disorder Chorea Acanthocytosis.
source: The VPS13A gene is associated with the neurodegenerative disorder Chorea Acanthocytosis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: VPS13A is a peripheral membrane protein.
source: We demonstrate that VPS13A is a peripheral membrane protein, associated with mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical fractionation experiments shown in Figure 1 and described in the Results section.

claim: VPS13A is associated with mitochondria.
source: We demonstrate that VPS13A is a peripheral membrane protein, associated with mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-localization studies with mitochondrial markers (Figure 2C) and fractionation experiments (Figure 1D).

claim: VPS13A is associated with the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: We demonstrate that VPS13A is a peripheral membrane protein, associated with mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets.
evidence: This is shown through co-localization with ER markers VAP-A and Sec61B (Figure 3A-C).

claim: VPS13A is associated with lipid droplets.
source: We demonstrate that VPS13A is a peripheral membrane protein, associated with mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-localization with lipid droplet markers BODIPY-FA and LipidTox (Figure 6A-C).

claim: VPS13A is localized at sites where the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria are in close contact.
source: VPS13A is localized at sites where the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria are in close contact.
evidence: This is shown through co-localization studies with both ER and mitochondrial markers (Figure 3B-C).

claim: VPS13A interacts with the ER residing protein VAP-A via its FFAT domain.
source: VPS13A interacts with the ER residing protein VAP-A via its FFAT domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4B) and in vitro binding assays (Figure 4D).

claim: Interaction of VPS13A with mitochondria is mediated via its C-terminal domain.
source: Interaction with mitochondria is mediated via its C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is shown through localization studies of VPS13A fragments, where the C-terminal region (aa 2615-3174) localizes to mitochondria (Figure 2E).

claim: In VPS13A-depleted cells, ER-mitochondria contact sites are decreased.
source: In VPS13A-depleted cells, ER-mitochondria contact sites are decreased, mitochondria are fragmented and mitophagy is decreased.
evidence: This is demonstrated using the SPLICS assay in VPS13A KO cells (Figure 5A-B).

claim: In VPS13A-depleted cells, mitochondria are fragmented.
source: In VPS13A-depleted cells, ER-mitochondria contact sites are decreased, mitochondria are fragmented and mitophagy is decreased.
evidence: This is shown through morphological analysis of mitochondria in VPS13A KO cells (Figure 5C).

claim: In VPS13A-depleted cells, mitophagy is decreased.
source: In VPS13A-depleted cells, ER-mitochondria contact sites are decreased, mitochondria are fragmented and mitophagy is decreased.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mitophagy assays using CCCP and Parkin overexpression (Figure 5D).

claim: VPS13A localizes to lipid droplets.
source: VPS13A also localizes to lipid droplets and affects lipid droplet motility.
evidence: This is shown through co-localization with lipid droplet markers (Figure 6A-C) and fractionation studies (Figure 7).

claim: VPS13A affects lipid droplet motility.
source: VPS13A also localizes to lipid droplets and affects lipid droplet motility.
evidence: This is demonstrated through live cell imaging showing reduced motility of VPS13A-positive lipid droplets (Figure 8E-F, Video 3).

claim: In VPS13A-depleted mammalian cells lipid droplet numbers are increased.
source: In VPS13A-depleted mammalian cells lipid droplet numbers are increased.
evidence: This is shown through quantification of lipid droplets in VPS13A KO cells (Figure 8A-C).

claim: VPS13A is required for establishing membrane contact sites between various organelles to enable lipid transfer required for mitochondria and lipid droplet related processes.
source: Our data, together with recently published data from others, indicate that VPS13A is required for establishing membrane contact sites between various organelles to enable lipid transfer required for mitochondria and lipid droplet related processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and integration with published literature.

claim: The vertebrate VPS13 protein family consists of four closely related proteins, VPS13A, VPS13B, VPS13C and VPS13D.
source: The vertebrate VPS13 protein family consists of four closely related proteins, VPS13A, VPS13B, VPS13C and VPS13D (Velayos-Baeza et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: Mutations in VPS13B, VPS13C and VPS13D are associated with the onset of neurological and developmental disorders.
source: Mutations in VPS13B, VPS13C and VPS13D are associated with the onset of neurological and developmental disorders (Kolehmainen et al., 2003; Seifert et al., 2009; Lesage et al., 2016; Gauthier et al., 2018; Seong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to support it.

claim: Mutations in the VPS13A gene are causative for a specific autosomal recessive neurological disorder, Chorea Acanthocytosis (ChAc).
source: Mutations in the VPS13A gene are causative for a specific autosomal recessive neurological disorder, Chorea Acanthocytosis (ChAc) (Rampoldi et al., 2001; Ueno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Most reported VPS13A mutations in ChAc patients result in low levels or absence of the protein.
source: Most reported VPS13A mutations in ChAc patients result in low levels or absence of the protein (Dobson-Stone et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: ChAc patients display gradual onset of hyperkinetic movements and cognitive abnormalities.
source: ChAc patients display gradual onset of hyperkinetic movements and cognitive abnormalities (Hermann and Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: VPS13A is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues.
source: The function of VPS13A may not be restricted to the brain but also to other tissues since VPS13A is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues (Velayos-Baeza et al., 2004; Rampoldi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: In yeast, Vps13 is a peripheral membrane protein localized at membrane contact sites including nucleus-vacuole, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-vacuole and endosome-mitochondria contact sites.
source: In yeast, Vps13 is a peripheral membrane protein localized at membrane contact sites including nucleus-vacuole, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-vacuole and endosome-mitochondria contact sites (Park et al., 2016; Lang et al., 2015; John Peter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Vps13 mutants are synthetically lethal with mutations in genes required to form the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) complex.
source: Vps13 mutants are synthetically lethal with mutations in genes required to form the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) complex (Park et al., 2016; Lang et al., 2015), suggesting a redundant role of Vps13 at membrane contact sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Vps13 is involved in the transport of membrane bound proteins between the trans-Golgi network and prevacuolar compartment (PVC).
source: In addition, Vps13 is involved in the transport of membrane bound proteins between the trans-Golgi network and prevacuolar compartment (PVC) (Redding et al., 1996; Brickner and Fuller, 1997) and from endosome to vacuole (Luo and Chang, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Vps13 is involved in the transport of membrane bound proteins from endosome to vacuole.
source: In addition, Vps13 is involved in the transport of membrane bound proteins between the trans-Golgi network and prevacuolar compartment (PVC) (Redding et al., 1996; Brickner and Fuller, 1997) and from endosome to vacuole (Luo and Chang, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Vps13 is required for prospore expansion, cytokinesis, mitochondria integrity, membrane contacts and homotypic fusion.
source: Vps13 is also required for prospore expansion, cytokinesis, mitochondria integrity, membrane contacts and homotypic fusion and the influential role of Vps13 in these processes is postulated to be dependent on the availability of phosphatidylinositides (Park et al., 2016; Lang et al., 2015; John Peter et al., 2017; Park and Neiman, 2012; Nakanishi et al., 2007; De et al., 2017; Rzepnikowska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: The VPS13A gene is located at chromosome 9q21.
source: The VPS13A gene is located at chromosome 9q21 and encodes a high molecular weight protein of 3174 amino acids (Velayos-Baeza et al., 2004; Rampoldi et al., 2001; Ueno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: VPS13A encodes a high molecular weight protein of 3174 amino acids.
source: The VPS13A gene is located at chromosome 9q21 and encodes a high molecular weight protein of 3174 amino acids (Velayos-Baeza et al., 2004; Rampoldi et al., 2001; Ueno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Loss of VPS13A is associated with impaired autophagic degradation.
source: In various model systems, loss of VPS13A is associated with diverse phenotypes, such as impaired autophagic degradation, defective protein homeostasis (Muñoz-Braceras et al., 2015; Lupo et al., 2016; Vonk et al., 2017), delayed endocytic and phagocytic processing (Korolchuk et al., 2007; Samaranayake et al., 2011), actin polymerization defects (Föller et al., 2012; Alesutan et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013; Honisch et al., 2015) and abnormal calcium homeostasis (Yu et al., 2016; Pelzl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Loss of VPS13A is associated with defective protein homeostasis.
source: In various model systems, loss of VPS13A is associated with diverse phenotypes, such as impaired autophagic degradation, defective protein homeostasis (Muñoz-Braceras et al., 2015; Lupo et al., 2016; Vonk et al., 2017), delayed endocytic and phagocytic processing (Korolchuk et al., 2007; Samaranayake et al., 2011), actin polymerization defects (Föller et al., 2012; Alesutan et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013; Honisch et al., 2015) and abnormal calcium homeostasis (Yu et al., 2016; Pelzl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Loss of VPS13A is associated with delayed endocytic and phagocytic processing.
source: In various model systems, loss of VPS13A is associated with diverse phenotypes, such as impaired autophagic degradation, defective protein homeostasis (Muñoz-Braceras et al., 2015; Lupo et al., 2016; Vonk et al., 2017), delayed endocytic and phagocytic processing (Korolchuk et al., 2007; Samaranayake et al., 2011), actin polymerization defects (Föller et al., 2012; Alesutan et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013; Honisch et al., 2015) and abnormal calcium homeostasis (Yu et al., 2016; Pelzl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Loss of VPS13A is associated with actin polymerization defects.
source: In various model systems, loss of VPS13A is associated with diverse phenotypes, such as impaired autophagic degradation, defective protein homeostasis (Muñoz-Braceras et al., 2015; Lupo et al., 2016; Vonk et al., 2017), delayed endocytic and phagocytic processing (Korolchuk et al., 2007; Samaranayake et al., 2011), actin polymerization defects (Föller et al., 2012; Alesutan et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013; Honisch et al., 2015) and abnormal calcium homeostasis (Yu et al., 2016; Pelzl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Loss of VPS13A is associated with abnormal calcium homeostasis.
source: In various model systems, loss of VPS13A is associated with diverse phenotypes, such as impaired autophagic degradation, defective protein homeostasis (Muñoz-Braceras et al., 2015; Lupo et al., 2016; Vonk et al., 2017), delayed endocytic and phagocytic processing (Korolchuk et al., 2007; Samaranayake et al., 2011), actin polymerization defects (Föller et al., 2012; Alesutan et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013; Honisch et al., 2015) and abnormal calcium homeostasis (Yu et al., 2016; Pelzl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Proteomic studies revealed that VPS13A is associated with multiple cellular organelles.
source: Proteomic studies revealed that VPS13A is associated with multiple cellular organelles (Huttlin et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2011; Hung et al., 2017) suggesting that VPS13A probably plays a role in a multitude of cellular functions and its loss of function could be associated with a wide range of cellular defects in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: VPS13A was enriched in the pellet fraction containing transmembrane proteins.
source: VPS13A was enriched in the pellet, which contained the transmembrane epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and relatively little of α-tubulin, a cytosolic marker protein (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through biochemical fractionation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Following digitonin treatment and centrifugation, more than 80% of VPS13A remained in the fraction containing membrane associated proteins.
source: Following digitonin treatment and centrifugation, more than 80% of VPS13A, remained in the fraction containing membrane associated proteins such as EGFR and the ER integral protein- VAMP-associated protein A (VAP-A), and little VPS13A was detected in the cytosolic non-membrane bound and GAPDH containing fraction (Figure 1B and B').
evidence: This is demonstrated through digitonin-based fractionation shown in Figure 1B and B'.

claim: Part of VPS13A was solubilized by alkaline and urea-containing solutions, similar to ATP5A, a peripheral membrane associated protein.
source: Similarly to ATP5A, a peripheral membrane associated protein of mitochondria, part of VPS13A was solubilized by alkaline and urea-containing solutions. In contrast, the integral membrane protein EGFR was not solubilized by alkaline containing solutions and was, as expected, only partly removed by urea containing solutions (Figure 1C,C').
evidence: This is demonstrated through chemical extraction experiments shown in Figure 1C and C'.

claim: VPS13A was predominantly detected in fractions containing VAP-A, Rab7 and ATP5A in sucrose gradient fractionation.
source: These experiments showed that VPS13A was predominantly detected in fractions containing VAP-A, Rab7 and ATP5A, which are marker proteins of the ER, endosomes and mitochondria respectively (Figure 1D,D').
evidence: This is demonstrated through sucrose gradient fractionation shown in Figure 1D and D'.

claim: VPS13A-GFP strongly decorated the periphery of nearly all mitochondria stained with Mitotracker.
source: VPS13A-GFP strongly decorated the periphery of nearly all mitochondria stained with Mitotracker (Figure 2C,C', C" and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2C and Video 1.

claim: The C-terminal region of VPS13A (aa 2615–3174) showed a localization pattern similar to that of the mitochondrial outer membrane marker TOMM20.
source: Most of these constructs showed an apparently cytosolic distribution pattern except, the C-terminal region of VPS13A (aa 2615–3174) which showed a localization pattern similar to that of the mitochondrial outer membrane marker TOMM20 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through localization studies of VPS13A fragments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: VPS13A was highly enriched in the mitochondria fraction.
source: VPS13A was highly enriched in the mitochondria fraction and slightly in the microsomal (pellet) fraction (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: VPS13A was found in the soluble supernatant following Na2CO3 treatment, similar to ATP5A.
source: While TOMM20 was mostly retained in the insoluble membrane fraction following Na2CO3 treatment, VPS13A was now also found in the soluble supernatant in a similar way as ATP5A (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through alkaline extraction experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: When crude mitochondria fractions were treated with proteinase K (PK), both TOMM20 and VPS13A were stripped off.
source: Moreover, when crude mitochondria fractions were treated with proteinase K (PK), both TOMM20 and VPS13A were stripped off, suggesting that VPS13A is exposed to the cytosol (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through proteinase K treatment experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The VPS13A localization pattern partly overlapped with the ER markers VAP-A and BFP-Sec61B.
source: Furthermore, the VPS13A localization pattern partly overlapped with the ER markers VAP-A and BFP-Sec61B (yellow signal in Figure 3A, white arrowheads in Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-localization studies shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: VPS13A-GFP was closely associated to VAP-A positive regions of the ER.
source: This analysis showed that VPS13A-GFP was closely associated to VAP-A positive regions of the ER, the signals partially overlapped, and the dynamics of the VPS13A positive regions are similar to the ER dynamics (Figure 3D and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3D and Video 2.

claim: VAP-A was enriched in immunoprecipitates of endogenous VPS13A.
source: In line with this hypothesis, VAP-A was enriched in immunoprecipitates of endogenous VPS13A (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: VPS13A was present in the VAP-A immunoprecipitates.
source: Conversely, VPS13A was present in the VAP-A immunoprecipitates (Figure 4B').
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4B'.

claim: All the constructs containing the VPS13A FFAT motif were efficiently binding VAP-A.
source: We found that all the constructs containing the VPS13A FFAT motif were efficiently binding VAP-A (Figure 4D), including the FFAT motif itself (Figure 4D, Lane 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro pull-down experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The introduction of the D845A point mutation in the FFAT motif reduced its association to VAP-A.
source: Importantly, the introduction of the D845A point mutation in this motif, which is known to affect VAP-A binding in other FFAT-containing proteins (Loewen et al., 2003; Saita et al., 2009), reduced its association to VAP-A (Figure 4D, Lane 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro pull-down experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: VPS13A∆FFAT still presented co-localization to mitochondria comparable to the full length.
source: Analysis of confocal images showed that VPS13A∆FFAT still presented co-localization to mitochondria comparable to the full length (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, yellow signal in the overlay images) but no co-localization was observed between ER-marker VAP-A and VPS13A∆FFAT (absence of yellow signal in the overlay image of VPS13A∆FFAT and VAP-A, (Figure 4E', Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the FFAT domain is the main hub for ER targeting of VPS13A.
evidence: This is demonstrated through localization studies shown in Figure 4E' and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: No co-localization was observed between ER-marker VAP-A and VPS13A∆FFAT.
source: Analysis of confocal images showed that VPS13A∆FFAT still presented co-localization to mitochondria comparable to the full length (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, yellow signal in the overlay images) but no co-localization was observed between ER-marker VAP-A and VPS13A∆FFAT (absence of yellow signal in the overlay image of VPS13A∆FFAT and VAP-A, (Figure 4E', Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the FFAT domain is the main hub for ER targeting of VPS13A.
evidence: This is demonstrated through localization studies shown in Figure 4E' and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: VPS13A-GFPΔFFAT did not immunoprecipitate with endogenous VAP-A, whereas the full length construct did.
source: To further investigate the requirement of the FFAT domain in the interaction with VAP-A, we expressed VPS13A-GFPΔFFAT and found no immunoprecipitation with endogenous VAP-A, whereas the full length construct did (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GFP-trap assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: An increased amount of endogenous VPS13A bound to GFP-VAP-A was observed after TG treatment.
source: GFP-VAP-A was expressed in HeLa cells and after TG treatment GFP-trap assays were used to immunoprecipitate GFP-VAP-A and an increased amount of endogenous VPS13A bound to GFP-VAP-A was observed (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GFP-trap assays after thapsigargin treatment shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The increase in VPS13A-VAP-A interaction was proportional to the concentration of TG applied.
source: The increase was proportional to the concentration of TG applied.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of the GFP-trap assays shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Both signals from the SPLICS assay, for narrow and wide distances, are significantly decreased in VPS13A depleted cells compared to the parental cell line.
source: Both signals from the SPLICS assay, for narrow and wide distances, are significantly decreased in VPS13A depleted cells compared to the parental cell line (Figure 5A''–B").
evidence: This is demonstrated through the SPLICS assay shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: VPS13A depleted cells contained less elongated mitochondria compared to control cells when cultured under standard conditions.
source: Upon morphological examination we found that VPS13A depleted cells contained less elongated mitochondria compared to control cells when cultured under standard conditions (Figure 5C,C').
evidence: This is demonstrated through morphological analysis shown in Figure 5C and C'.

claim: Upon starvation, an increased amount of VPS13A KO cells with elongated mitochondria was observed, however, not to the extent as observed in control cells.
source: Upon starvation, a process which induces the formation of elongated mitochondria (Rambold et al., 2011), an increased amount of VPS13A KO cells with elongated mitochondria was observed, however, not to the extent as observed in control cells (Figure 5C,C').
evidence: This is demonstrated through morphological analysis after starvation shown in Figure 5C and C'.

claim: A reduced capacity to eliminate damaged mitochondria by mitophagy was observed in the KO cell line.
source: Finally, a reduced capacity to eliminate damaged mitochondria by mitophagy was observed in the KO cell line, after inducing mitophagy with CCCP and overexpression of Parkin (Narendra et al., 2008) (Figure 5D) together with an increase in S616 phosphorylation of Drp1, a phosphorylation associated with decreased fusion and increased fission (Figure 5E–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) (Rambold et al., 2011; Kashatus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mitophagy assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: An increase in S616 phosphorylation of Drp1 was observed in VPS13A KO cells.
source: Finally, a reduced capacity to eliminate damaged mitochondria by mitophagy was observed in the KO cell line, after inducing mitophagy with CCCP and overexpression of Parkin (Narendra et al., 2008) (Figure 5D) together with an increase in S616 phosphorylation of Drp1, a phosphorylation associated with decreased fusion and increased fission (Figure 5E–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) (Rambold et al., 2011; Kashatus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: VPS13A positive structures co-localized with lipid droplet specific dyes BODIPY-FA or LipidTox red.
source: Using confocal microscopy with lipid droplets (LDs) specific dyes, BODIPY-FA or LipidTox red, we showed that the VPS13A positive structures co-localized with these dyes, indicating that these VPS13A positive vesicular-like structures were LDs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Line scan analysis of individual large LDs revealed that VPS13A-GFP uniformly encircled them.
source: Line scan analysis of individual large LDs at a high magnification revealed that VPS13A-GFP uniformly encircled them (Figure 6C,C'), indicating enrichment of VPS13A at the membrane and not at the interior of LDs, the ring-like VPS13A positive signal is most obvious at the periphery of larger LDs (such as after 120' OA, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through line scan analysis shown in Figure 6C and C'.

claim: Induction of LD formation after incubation of cells with OA for 24 hr resulted in a shift in the distribution of endogenous VPS13A towards the LD fraction.
source: Induction of LD formation after incubation of cells with OA for 24 hr resulted in a shift in the distribution of endogenous VPS13A towards the LD fraction. As expected, PLIN2 was enriched in the top fraction consistent with the fact that LDs are formed in response to OA induction (Figure 7B,B' and B", Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sucrose gradient fractionation shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Addition of OA to starved cells increased the amount of VPS13A in the LD fraction.
source: In addition, comparison of the amount of VPS13A in the LD fraction showed that VPS13A was partly concentrated in the LD fractions of OA fed cells. Addition of OA to starved cells increased the amount of VPS13A in the LD fraction (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sucrose gradient fractionation shown in Figure 7C.

claim: VPS13A-GFP∆FFAT was recruited to LDs similarly as WT VPS13A-GFP.
source: To do so, we expressed VPS13A-GFP∆FFAT in OA fed cells and showed that it was recruited to LDs similarly as WT VPS13A-GFP (Figure 7D,D').
evidence: This is demonstrated through localization studies shown in Figure 7D and D'.

claim: Under normal culturing conditions, VPS13A KO cells showed increased numbers of LDs compared to the parental control line.
source: Under normal culturing conditions, VPS13A KO cells showed increased numbers of LDs (Figure 8A–B) compared to the parental control line.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of LDs shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: FACS quantification of the total Nile red intensity showed a significantly increased intensity in the absence of VPS13A.
source: In addition, fluorescent activated cell sorting (FACS) quantification of the total Nile red intensity showed a significantly increased intensity in the absence of VPS13A (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through FACS analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: OA induction in VPS13A KO cells resulted in an increase in LDs comparable to control cells.
source: VPS13A is not required for LD formation, because VPS13KO cells do contain LDs and OA induction in VPS13A KO cells resulted in an increase in LDs comparable to control cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of LDs after OA induction shown in Figure 8D.

claim: VPS13A-GFP positive LDs slowly and randomly oscillated.
source: Visual examination showed that VPS13A-GFP positive LDs slowly and randomly oscillated. When these LDs were briefly dissociated from VPS13A-GFP, they directionally traveled faster and such motility was interrupted when VPS13A-GFP was again associated with the LD (Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live cell imaging shown in Video 3.

claim: In VPS13A-GFP overexpressing cells, a larger fraction of the LDs showed an overlapping pattern compared to the non-transfected cells.
source: In VPS13A-GFP overexpressing cells, a larger fraction of the LDs showed an overlapping pattern compared to the non-transfected cells (Figure 8E–F), further suggesting that VPS13A overexpression reduces LD motility.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of LD motility shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: 5 day old Vps13 mutants have increased numbers of LDs compared to wildtype.
source: Examination of the eyes using Nile red to visualize LDs showed that 5 day old Vps13 mutants have increased numbers of LDs compared to wildtype (Figure 9A–C').
evidence: This is demonstrated through Nile red staining of Drosophila eyes shown in Figure 9A-C'.

claim: Overexpression of human VPS13A in the Drosophila Vps13 mutant background rescued the LD phenotype back to normal.
source: Overexpression of human VPS13A in the mutant background (Figure 9D–E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) rescued the phenotype back to normal.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Nile red staining and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 9D-E.

claim: Drosophila Vps13 and human VPS13A share functional properties.
source: These data indicate that Drosophila Vps13 and human VPS13A share functional properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that human VPS13A can rescue the Drosophila Vps13 mutant phenotype.

claim: The peripheral membrane characteristics of VPS13A are shared by the other human VPS13 proteins (B, C and D), the yeast and the Drosophila Vps13 protein.
source: The peripheral membrane characteristics of VPS13A are shared by the other human VPS13 proteins (B, C and D), the yeast and the Drosophila Vps13 protein (Lesage et al., 2016; Brickner and Fuller, 1997; Vonk et al., 2017; Velayos-Baeza et al., 2008; Seifert et al., 2011), suggesting a common feature of VPS13 proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: VAP-A/B proteins have been extensively characterized as a hub when the ER establishes membrane contacts with other organelles including endosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, plasma membrane and Golgi.
source: VAP-A/B proteins have been extensively characterized as a hub when the ER establishes membrane contacts with other organelles including endosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, plasma membrane and Golgi (Alpy et al., 2013; Eden et al., 2016; Costello et al., 2017; Hua et al., 2017; Stoica et al., 2014; Gomez-Suaga et al., 2017; Mesmin et al., 2013; Stefan et al., 2011; Rocha et al., 2009; Dong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: VPS13A also interacts with VAP-B in a FFAT dependent manner.
source: Our results showed that VPS13A also interacts with VAP-B in a FFAT dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3), consistent with the fact that VAP-A and VAP-B functions are often redundant (Dong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: The observed interaction between VPS13A and VAP-A in a FFAT-dependent manner and the reported localization at the ER-mitochondria contact sites is consistent with localization studies recently reported by Kumar et al.
source: Our observed interaction between VPS13A and VAP-A in a FFAT-dependent manner and our reported localization at the ER-mitochondria contact sites is consistent with localization studies recently reported by Kumar et al (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: ER-mitochondria contact sites are decreased in VPS13A depleted cells, consistent with results by Kumar et al, which demonstrate that upon overexpression of VPS13A an increase in ER-mitochondria contact sites is observed.
source: We further show that ER-mitochondria contact sites are decreased in VPS13A depleted cells, consistent with results by Kumar et al, which demonstrate that upon overexpression of VPS13A an increase in ER-mitochondria contact sites is observed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: The data and the data by Kumar et al are in line with studies in yeast demonstrating that Vps13 is present at various organelle contact sites and is required for ER-mitochondria contact sites, all pointing to a conserved function of VPS13A at these sites.
source: Our data and the data by Kumar et al are in line with studies in yeast demonstrating that Vps13 is present at various organelle contact sites and is required for ER-mitochondria contact sites, all pointing to a conserved function of VPS13A at these sites.

claim: The reported mitochondria phenotypes (less elongated and a decreased mitophagy capacity) in the VPS13A depleted cells could all be explained by abnormal lipid composition of mitochondria membranes.
source: Our reported mitochondria phenotypes (less elongated and a decreased mitophagy capacity) in the VPS13A depleted cells could all be explained by abnormal lipid composition of mitochondria membranes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion.

claim: A possible defect in lipid transfer between ER and mitochondria due to VPS13A depletion is in line with results from Kumar et al., who demonstrated in vitro that the N-terminal part of yeast Vps13, which is highly similar to human VPS13A, is able to transfer lipids between two membranes.
source: A possible defect in lipid transfer between ER and mitochondria due to VPS13A depletion is in line with results from Kumar et al., who demonstrated in vitro that the N-terminal part of yeast Vps13, which is highly similar to human VPS13A, is able to transfer lipids between two membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: Human VPS13A plays a role in tethering ER to the outer membrane of mitochondria to create areas of close proximity and to enable transfer of lipids between these membranes via the VPS13A N-terminal domain.
source: Together, these data favor a model in which human VPS13A plays a role in tethering ER to the outer membrane of mitochondria to create areas of close proximity and to enable transfer of lipids between these membranes via the VPS13A N-terminal domain (Figure 10A,C).
evidence: This is a model proposed in the discussion based on the experimental data and published literature.

claim: VPS13A localizes to the periphery of LDs in a FFAT-independent manner, consistent with the recent report from Kumar et al.
source: In addition to the localization at ER-mitochondria contact sites, VPS13A localizes to the periphery of LDs in a FFAT-independent manner, consistent with the recent report from Kumar et al (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: Bean et al. have recently shown in yeast that different adaptor proteins present at specific subcellular locations compete for binding to Vps13.
source: Bean et al. (Bean et al., 2018) have recently shown in yeast that different adaptor proteins present at specific subcellular locations compete for binding to Vps13.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: Organelle-specific VPS13A adaptor proteins may be present in mammalian cells.
source: Organelle-specific VPS13A adaptor proteins may be present as well in mammalian cells; LD specific adaptor proteins would increase in conditions when LDs are increased, resulting in enhanced competition for VPS13A which could possibly be relocated to LDs from other sub-cellular locations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion.

claim: VPS13A influences the motility of LDs, a feature reminiscent of identified proteins regulating dynamics of endosomal vesicles.
source: VPS13A influences the motility of LDs, a feature reminiscent of identified proteins regulating dynamics of endosomal vesicles.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Endosomal movement is halted when endosomes make contacts with the ER.
source: Endosomal movement is halted when endosomes make contacts with the ER (Raiborg et al., 2015) and movement of peroxisomes is increased upon loss of the VAP-ACBD5 tethering complex (Costello et al., 2017; Hua et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: Movement of peroxisomes is increased upon loss of the VAP-ACBD5 tethering complex.
source: Endosomal movement is halted when endosomes make contacts with the ER (Raiborg et al., 2015) and movement of peroxisomes is increased upon loss of the VAP-ACBD5 tethering complex (Costello et al., 2017; Hua et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: VPS13A negatively influences LD motility and LDs are more fixed under conditions of VPS13A overexpression.
source: Consistent with this, we show that VPS13A negatively influences LD motility and LDs are more fixed under conditions of VPS13A overexpression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the data shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: Increased numbers of LDs in VPS13A depleted cells can be explained because in the absence of VPS13A the association with the ER may be reduced and lipid transfer decreased.
source: Increased numbers of LDs in VPS13A depleted cells can be explained because in the absence of VPS13A the association with the ER may be reduced and lipid transfer decreased. This in turn could lead to disruption of LD turnover processes such as lipophagy and release of LD content to other organelles (Rambold et al., 2015; Kaushik and Cuervo, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: The increased numbers of LDs in glia cells of the fly Vps13 mutant eyes could be caused by an initial impairment in mitochondrial function.
source: Thus, it is possible that the increased numbers of LDs in glia cells of the fly Vps13 mutant eyes could be caused by an initial impairment in mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion.

claim: Impairment of mitochondria processes such as fusion and mitophagy could explain the neurodegeneration observed in ChAc patients, since impairment of these processes has been largely linked to neurodegeneration.
source: Impairment of mitochondria processes such as fusion and mitophagy could explain the neurodegeneration observed in ChAc patients, since impairment of these processes has been largely linked to neurodegeneration (Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: Impairment of LD related processes could explain neurodegeneration as well since LD abnormalities are associated with several neurodegenerative diseases such as hereditary spastic paraplegias, Huntington's disease, and Parkinson's disease.
source: In addition, impairment of LD related processes could explain neurodegeneration as well since LD abnormalities are associated with several neurodegenerative diseases such as hereditary spastic paraplegias (Inloes et al., 2014), Huntington's disease (Martinez-Vicente et al., 2010), and Parkinson's disease (Outeiro and Lindquist, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: VPS13A contains a putative FFAT motif located between amino acids 842–848.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support it.

claim: In response to impaired mitochondria function in neuronal cells of the Drosophila eye, ROS levels increase and lipids are transferred from neurons to glia cells where LDs transiently form.
source: It has been reported that, in response to impaired mitochondria function in neuronal cells of the Drosophila eye, ROS levels increase and lipids are transferred from neurons to glia cells where LDs transiently form (Liu et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017).

claim: An increase in LDs in glia cells in response to impaired mitochondria functioning is also observed in neurodegenerative mouse models.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: VPS13A does not co-localize with the endosomal/lysosomal marker proteins Rab5, Rab7, LAMP1 and FYCO1.
source: Although not co-localizing with the endosomal/lysosomal marker proteins Rab5, Rab7, LAMP1 and FYCO1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2), VPS13A-GFP strongly decorated the periphery of nearly all mitochondria stained with Mitotracker (Figure 2C,C', C" and Video 1).

claim: VPS13A co-fractionates with TOMM20, a protein localized at the outer membrane of mitochondria.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the fractionation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The FFAT domain appeared not to be sufficient for an in vivo association with the ER, since FFAT containing VPS13A fragments appeared to remain cytosolic and did not show a reticular pattern.
source: The FFAT domain appeared not to be sufficient for an in vivo association with the ER, since FFAT containing VPS13A fragments appeared to remain cytosolic and did not show a reticular pattern (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is supported by the localization data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The assembly of membrane contact sites is regulated by cellular calcium levels.
source: The assembly of membrane contact sites is regulated by cellular calcium levels (Giordano et al., 2013; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to support it.

claim: Calcium levels are mainly regulated through the activity of sarcoendoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA), which can be pharmacologically inhibited with thapsigargin (TG), leading to an increase in cytosolic calcium.
source: Calcium levels are mainly regulated through the activity of sarcoendoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA), which can be pharmacologically inhibited with thapsigargin (TG), leading to an increase in cytosolic calcium.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is based on established knowledge.

claim: The calcium mediated VPS13A-VAP-A interaction suggests that VPS13A plays a role in ER-mitochondria contact sites.
source: The calcium mediated VPS13A-VAP-A interaction suggests that VPS13A plays a role in ER-mitochondria contact sites.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: VPS13A can associate simultaneously with mitochondria and ER via its C-terminus and FFAT domain, respectively.
source: In conclusion, our data support a model where VPS13A can associate simultaneously with mitochondria and ER via its C-terminus and FFAT domain, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A MCR5 VPS13A KO cell line was obtained via a CRISPR/Cas9 approach, with no detectable levels of VPS13A protein while its closest homologous protein VPS13C appears normal.
source: In order to investigate a possible role of VPS13A in ER-mitochondria contact sites, we used a MCR5 VPS13A KO cell line, obtained via a CRISPR/Cas9 approach, with no detectable levels of VPS13A protein while its closest homologous protein VPS13C appears normal (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).

source: Different VPS13 members may have their own specific adaptor proteins which would explain their different reported localizations, such as VPS13B at the Golgi (Seifert et al., 2011) or VPS13C at endosomes (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation provided in the discussion with citations to support it.

claim: Since different VPS13 proteins can localize at the same organelles, such as VPS13A and VPS13C in LDs and mitochondria, it is also possible that the same adaptor protein could bind several VPS13 proteins.

source: Given the described functions of VPS13A in tethering ER-mitochondria membranes and transferring lipids, it could be expected that VPS13A at LDs is probably performing a comparable function.
